facts.fact: Millhaven has a mill and a stone storehouse for grain; sacks are chalk-tallied along the seam (rows of five struck through); a bin and a tally board hold the day's count.

Millhaven has an established grain seller (Mister Hollis) and a newer, cheaper one; households argue over the price. Every village south of the Pass has 'a new man with a cart once a season' (Sylvanas's inference).

The old carter says he comes up to the mill every fortnight with an empty wagon and goes home full; barley is up a copper the measure in the south and people are crying about it but buying; the market at the ford was busy 'yesterday'. 'You'll get a better price going home full than going home empty' (Lyriel's idiom).
Farm economy: ploughland, barley stubble and stooks in autumn; market day at Millhaven; tinkers mend pots; wheelwright, smith and mill are the village trades.

The sick village's grain and bread chain: valley farms (for twenty years) -> granary keeper Joss -> bakehouse (all its flour from the granary), plus granary flour to most houses on the near side of the brook and the top farm since harvest (its own barley rotted wet and black in the ear). Three months ago a new young man with a cart from the west road undercut the farms by two coppers on the measure (barley and flour); Joss bought four loads, the last a fortnight ago; sacks stencilled with a wheat sheaf in a ring and ANDORHAL; most of the last load was in the loft.

Bread is the staple: the cooper's house of five buys two loaves a day from the bakehouse (Ellen's mam) and eats bread with everything; Ashby's buys bread and cheese from the village for field hands, 'cheaper than feeding the oven'; the baker's loaves are carried round by Ellen in a basket; Hallams and the alehouse took flour by cart (two sacks at the alehouse).

Andorhal's granaries supply the south; Brask's own barley goes through Andorhal. Brask orders the new man's flour burned in every house: a village loses a season of bread, the granary and the bakehouse in one night.

Grain depots log loads by day, carter, destination, sacks, weight off the beam and rate; free ('own cart') carters buy in the yard and sell where they like; the yard books the load, not the man, and is paid at the gate. Weights go on the carter's word and are settled at Andorhal.

Short-rate loads: twelve sacks at two coppers under the measure, from midsummer; Millhaven's the first (north road earliest by a fortnight); by road before/since last month: north 9/3, west 7/4, south 11/6, east 1/9; 31 places in Corley's book, 47 across the books (19 in more than one); Andorhal at one end of all 53 readable burned waybill halves (9 more burned through), Barov on 31.
A miller of thirty years has never known a carter buy back flour; a hamlet shop's notch-stick records cheap flour owed since midsummer.
Army requisitions at 'the King's price' have emptied remounts and oats in the river valley.

Chapter 6: Andorhal's granary quarter is working at full pace: tall timber granaries on stone feet with hoist beams, sacks going up on ropes, wagons queued at the gates, bake ovens, a mill wheel. Grain dust hangs over the quarter.

Chapter 6: the army's wagons ride empty down and loaded up the south road to Strahnbrad; farm lanes feed carts of sacks into the road toward Andorhal; empty carts return. Hen crates, geese and ordinary farm traffic on the flat.

Chapter 6: Jaina recalls that a young man with a cart sold flour two coppers cheaper on the measure at the sick village, four loads, the last a fortnight before the party came; Corley's book has such loads going out on every road from his crossing.

Chapter 7: Andorhal's grain trade runs on seals and bills: each yard has a wax seal and a small drawn mark (Fenner's is a hook with two bars through the shank); the gate clerk matches a carter's bill to the seal board; guards spike sacks; the inspection office keeps the second copy of every bill that leaves; reeves write when a village sickens. A sealed, marked sample bag is kept from each flagged load. Forty-one copied marks since midsummer.

Chapter 7: the new supplier (a factor whose name is on contracts that nobody at the Exchange has met) took over Fenner's and the Exchange at high summer in the same week (new carters, new loaders), a little of Garside's at Lammas (dropped: 'the price was too good'), and Kett's and the weir-end malt-house the same month. Loaders are hired in from outside the town in pairs, sleep in the old rope-walk behind Fenner's (locks on both doors) and do not drink at the Wheatsheaf. Day crews go off at the Exchange bell at full dark; night crews go in; Kett's bills are for the first carts out.

Chapter 7: the sickness map: Mill Lane (Holt's, Fenner's, the Exchange granary, Garside's) and streets buying bread from the bakers at the bottom; old and babies first; a cough, thinning, one morning they do not get up; physicians say 'the river damp'. Households that buy from different ovens differ.
